drills.q: Explain mechanically why standard shuffled k-fold leaks on a fixed-horizon labeled time series, using the label-overlap correlation formula.
drills.a: label_t = sign(sum r_t+1..t+H) shares H-k of its H terms with label_t+k, giving theoretical correlation (H-k)/H -- e.g. 0.9 at lag 1 for H=10 -- with zero causal relationship. Random shuffling places near-duplicate-labeled neighbors on opposite sides of the split throughout the dataset, so any time-correlated feature can 'predict' the test label via that overlap rather than real signal.

drills.q: In a demonstration on i.i.d. noise returns (true accuracy 50%), naive shuffled 5-fold gave 85.9% accuracy, purged shuffled 5-fold gave 48.8% but had to discard 98% of training data, and sequential walk-forward with embargo gave 50.2% while discarding only 1-5%. What does the purge-fraction contrast imply about which base splitting scheme to use?
drills.a: It implies walk-forward should be the default base scheme, with purging/embargo layered on top for the residual boundary overlap -- not 'purge whatever random split you already had.' Needing to discard 98% of data to fix a self-inflicted leak is a sign the base split (random k-fold) was fundamentally the wrong tool, since walk-forward avoids creating that scale of overlap in the first place.

drills.q: Distinguish purging from embargo and give a concrete scenario where embargo specifically is needed beyond what purging (and walk-forward's past-only rule) already provides.
drills.a: Purging removes training samples whose windows overlap the test window, applied before the test block. Embargo is a buffer placed after the test block: a training sample resuming right after the test period can have a feature (e.g. a rolling stat) whose lookback window still reaches into the tail of the test period, leaking backward even though it's chronologically later and would otherwise pass the walk-forward 'past-only' rule.

drills.q: Derive why the Sharpe ratio estimator's variance formula includes skew and kurtosis terms rather than being just 1/T.
drills.a: Var[SR_hat] = [1 - skew*SR + ((kurt-1)/4)*SR^2]/(T-1) (Mertens 2002) reduces to ~1/T only when skew=0 and kurt=3 (normal returns). Real financial returns are typically negatively skewed and fat-tailed, inflating the bracket term, so treating Sharpe variance as 1/T understates true estimator uncertainty and overstates significance.

drills.q: A search of N=1000 strategy variants over T=250 daily observations reports a best annualized Sharpe of 1.5. Walk through why the Deflated Sharpe Ratio is only about 4.3%.
drills.a: E[max SR | N=1000, T=250, no real skill] ~= 3.27 annualized via the extreme-value formula -- pure luck across 1000 noise trials is expected to produce a best Sharpe more than double the observed 1.5. Plugging 1.5 against that 3.27 benchmark (instead of the naive 0) in the PSR formula gives a low z-score, so DSR ~= 0.043 -- only 4.3% probability of genuine skill.

drills.q: What's the most common way DSR gets computed correctly on paper but still misleads in practice?
drills.a: Undercounting N -- only including configurations that survived to the final report rather than every variant actually explored during iterative research (informal 'let's also try X' runs), which understates the correction and defeats the purpose of the metric.

drills.q: Compare expanding-window vs rolling-window walk-forward and state when you'd prefer each.
drills.a: Expanding window trains on all history (more data, but early folds are trained on much less data than late folds, and stale data can hurt if the regime shifted). Rolling window uses a fixed-size recent window (comparable data volume per fold, tests regime-sensitivity directly, but must be long enough to cover the phenomenon's real timescale). Prefer expanding when the phenomenon is stable over the full sample; prefer rolling when testing regime-sensitivity matters or old data is actively misleading.

drills.q: A colleague says 'walk-forward validation alone is sufficient, purging is only needed for shuffled k-fold.' Give a concrete counterexample.
drills.a: A walk-forward split with H=10-period-ahead labels, training block ending at t=500, test block starting at t=501: training samples at t=495-500 have label windows reaching to t=505-510, directly overlapping the first several test samples. Without purging those boundary training samples, the strictly-past-only walk-forward split still leaks label information into the test region.

drills.q: You inherit a strategy with a reported backtested Sharpe of 2.1 from 'proper walk-forward cross-validation,' one week before a capital allocation decision. What do you check, in priority order?
drills.a: First, verify the walk-forward split is genuinely sequential (no shuffling, no future data in feature construction) and that purging/embargo match the pipeline's actual label horizon and feature lookback windows -- leakage produces the largest, most misleading inflation. Second, reconstruct the true number of variants evaluated during research and recompute DSR honestly -- a Sharpe of 2.1 from hundreds of trials may not survive. Third, check the return series' skew/kurtosis feeding the Sharpe variance formula. Only then move to transaction costs, capacity, and market impact.

drills.q: Why does a good Deflated Sharpe Ratio not by itself mean a strategy is production-ready?
drills.a: DSR addresses statistical significance of the backtested Sharpe under multiple testing; it says nothing about transaction costs, market impact, capacity constraints, or regime shift after deployment -- those require separate diagnostics (market microstructure, risk metrics) even after a strategy clears the leakage and multiple-testing bars.
